scenes.title: Rows meet columns. Axes disappear.
scenes.description: Pick an output cell of C = A·B and watch its three products accumulate. Then reduce A over a named axis, keep or drop the reduced dimension, and compare the divisor of each mean.

cues.text: A is 2×3 and B is 3×2, so C = A·B is 2×2. Predict the chosen cell first.
Row i of A meets column j of B along the shared index r.
Multiply matching entries and add them into an accumulator, one r at a time.
The shared dimension is gone. State whether the loop starts from zero or from the first product.
A reduction also removes an axis. Say which one, and whether its size-1 dimension is kept.
A mean divides by the size of what was reduced. Averaging row sums is a different number.

accessibility.text: Matrix multiplication and reductions with the lesson's matrices. A has rows [1, 2, 3] and [4, 5, a] where a = A[1,2] defaults to 6; B has rows [1, 0], [0, 1] and [1, 1]. C[i,j] is the sum over r of A[i,r]·B[r,j], so C = [[4, 5], [10, 11]] by default and C[0,1] = 1·0 + 2·1 + 3·1 = 5. Each output needs three multiplications, twelve in total. Starting the accumulator from the first product needs two additions per output (eight in total); starting from a zero literal needs three (twelve). Summing A over axis 1 gives [6, 15] with shape (2,), or [[6], [15]] with shape (2,1) when the reduced dimension is kept; the means divide by 3. Over axis 0 the sums are [5, 7, 9], shape (3,), divisor 2. Over all axes the sum is 21 and the mean is 21/6 = 3.5, while the mean of the two row sums is 10.5, a different quantity. Changing a changes C[1,0], C[1,1] and every sum and mean that includes it.

scenes.title: Multiply the links. Then test the line.
scenes.description: Move w, x and a step δ. Follow the three local derivatives of the half squared error, multiply them into dL/dw, and compare the tangent-line prediction of a step with the exact loss.

nodes.text: p = w·x, r = p − y, L = r²/2

children.label: Drag or use arrows to change w

cues.text: Forward: prediction, residual, then the half squared error with target y = 5.
Three local links: dL/dr = r, dr/dp = 1 and dp/dw = x.
The chain rule multiplies them: dL/dw = r·x. A central difference agrees.
Predict the loss after a step δ with the tangent line: L + g·δ.
The exact loss differs by the omitted quadratic term, x²δ²/2.
Small steps make the line accurate; large steps measure the curve. With x = 0, w has no effect.

accessibility.text: Chain rule on one example with target y = 5. Prediction p = w·x, residual r = p − 5 and loss L = r²/2. The local derivatives are dL/dr = r, dr/dp = 1 and dp/dw = x, so dL/dw = r·x. At the lesson's x = 2, w = 1: p = 2, r = −3, L = 4.5 and dL/dw = −6, which a central difference with h = 0.00001 confirms. For a step δ = 0.01 the tangent line predicts 4.5 − 0.06 = 4.44, while the exact loss at w = 1.01 is 4.4402. The gap is always x²δ²/2, the quadratic term the line omits, so it is 0.0002 here and grows with the square of the step. The plot shows L(w) for w from 0 to 4, the tangent segment from w to w + δ and the exact value at w + δ. With x = 0 the weight cannot affect the prediction, so its gradient is zero.

scenes.title: Weight by count. Clear each window.
scenes.description: Two microbatches of different sizes contribute to one update. Change their sizes and mean gradients, compare count weighting with an equal average of means, and see what a buffer that is never cleared does to the next step.

cues.text: Both microbatches were computed at the same weight, w = 10. Predict the full-batch mean gradient.
Add the first contribution: its example count times its mean gradient.
Add the second contribution. No weight update happens between microbatches.
Divide by the total example count. An equal average of the two means ignores their sizes.
One optimizer step at the window boundary: w ← w − η·grad.
The next window contributes 2. A buffer that was not cleared still holds the old gradient.

accessibility.text: Gradient accumulation over two microbatches at weight 10 with learning rate 0.1. The lesson's case has 2 examples with mean gradient 3 and 1 example with mean gradient −3. Weighting each mean by its example count gives (2·3 + 1·(−3)) / 3 = 1, the full-batch mean, and the update gives w = 9.9. An equal average of the two means gives (3 − 3) / 2 = 0 and leaves w at 10. The two rules agree only when the microbatch sizes or their means are equal. The next accumulation window contributes 2: if the buffer was cleared the second update uses 2 and w becomes 9.7; if it was not, the buffer holds 1 + 2 = 3 and w becomes 9.6. Contributions are combined only between updates; updating after each microbatch would be several optimization steps, which this scene does not model.

scenes.title: A bend gates the gradient.
scenes.description: Feed two inputs through the lesson's two hidden units and one output. Watch ReLU block a negative preactivation in forward and its gradient in backward, then remove the nonlinearity and see the network collapse to one affine map.

cues.text: Weights are fixed: W1 rows [2, 1] and [−1, 2], b1 = [1, 0], v = [3, −1], output bias 0.5.
Each hidden preactivation is a dot product of a weight row with x, plus its bias.
ReLU keeps positive preactivations and replaces negative ones with zero.
Backward starts from the residual. Each hidden unit receives its output weight times r.
A closed gate passes no gradient: that unit's weight row and bias get zero for this example.
Without the nonlinearity, two affine layers equal one: 7·x1 + x2 + 3.5.

accessibility.text: A two-input, two-hidden-unit, one-output network with the lesson's weights: hidden rows [2, 1] and [−1, 2], hidden bias [1, 0], output weights [3, −1] and output bias 0.5, nine learned scalars in all. At x = [1, −2] the preactivations are [1, −5]; ReLU gives h = [1, 0] and the prediction is 3.5. With target 1 and half squared error, the residual is 2.5 and the loss 3.125. The hidden sensitivities are [7.5, −2.5]; ReLU passes the first and blocks the second, so the preactivation sensitivities are [7.5, 0], the first weight row's gradient is [7.5, −15], its bias gradient 7.5, and the output-weight gradients [2.5, 0]. This scene uses gradient 0 at exactly z = 0, a convention. Without the nonlinearity the network is the single affine map 7·x1 + x2 + 3.5 for every input; with ReLU it differs whenever a unit is shut.

scenes.title: Read the past. Never the answer.
scenes.description: Shift a four-token sequence into inputs and targets, choose an attention mask and a query row, and check whether that query can read its own target. Then choose how padded losses are averaged.

nodes.text: row i may read column j

cues.text: The full sequence is known during training. Predict which tokens each position may read.
Inputs drop the last token; targets drop the first, so position i predicts token i + 1.
The causal mask lets query i read keys j ≤ i: its own token and earlier ones.
Can the chosen query read the token it must predict? If so, training can copy the answer.
Change only token 7. Under a correct mask, earlier rows cannot move.
The loss averages valid targets. Padding slots and per-sequence means change the weighting.

accessibility.text: Teacher forcing on the sequence [4, 2, 7, 1]. Inputs are [4, 2, 7] and targets, shifted by one, are [2, 7, 1], so input position i predicts the token at position i + 1. A causal mask lets query i read key j when j ≤ i: query 0 reads only 4, query 1 reads 4 and 2, query 2 reads all three. No target is visible to its own query, so no row leaks. Without a mask, queries 0 and 1 can read the input position that holds their target (2 and 7), so two rows leak; a transposed mask (j ≥ i) also leaks there. Without the shift the target is the query's own input token, which every one of these masks allows: all three rows copy their answer. The future-token test changes only token 7 at key 2: under the causal mask only row 2 can change, while with no mask or a transposed mask rows 0 and 1 change too, which exposes the leak. For the loss, sequence A has token losses 1, 2 and 3; sequence B has one valid loss (default 4) and two padding slots. The valid-token mean is 10/4 = 2.5, dividing by all six slots gives about 1.667, and averaging the two sequence means gives 3.

scenes.title: Rotate both. Only the gap remains.
scenes.description: Rotate a query pair by m·θ and a key pair by n·θ. Their dot product equals the unrotated query against the key rotated by (n − m)·θ, so shifting both positions changes nothing unless the key was cached without its rotation. Then share KV heads across query heads.

nodes.text: R(α) rotates a pair by α

cues.text: One coordinate pair of a query and a key, before position is applied.
RoPE rotates the query pair by m·θ for query position m. Its length does not change.
The key pair rotates by n·θ for key position n.
The dot product of the rotated pair depends only on n − m. Shift both positions to check.
Grouped-query attention lets several query heads share one K/V head, shrinking K/V weights and cache.

accessibility.text: Rotary position embedding on one coordinate pair, with q = [2, 1] and k = [1, 3]. R(α) maps (a, b) to (a·cos α − b·sin α, a·sin α + b·cos α) and preserves length, so |R q| stays √5 ≈ 2.236. The query rotates by m·θ and the key by n·θ. Their dot product equals q · R((n − m)·θ) k, so it depends only on the position gap: with the defaults m = 1, n = 3 and θ = 30°, R q ≈ [1.232, 1.866], R k = [−3, 1] and both forms give about −1.83, and shifting both positions by one leaves it unchanged. If the key is cached without its rotation (the bug option), the product depends on m alone and no longer matches the relative form. The grouped-query panel uses width D = 8 split into four query heads of width 2: Q and the output projection have 64 parameters each, K and V have 8 × 2 × (KV heads) each. With two KV heads (q0, q1 share kv0; q2, q3 share kv1) the four projections total 192 parameters instead of 256 with four, and each token's K/V payload per layer is 8 values instead of 16. With one KV head the total is 160.

scenes.title: Pad the tail with the identity.
scenes.description: Sum the values 1 to n in fixed-size groups with a pairwise tree, then combine one partial per group. Change n, the group size and the sign pattern, and compare padding the final group with zeros against dropping it.

cues.text: Values 1 to n are split into groups of a fixed, invented size. Predict the total first.
The last group may be incomplete. Fill its empty slots with zero, the identity for addition.
Round 1: neighbouring slots add pairwise.
Each further round halves the slots: log2 of the group size rounds in all.
Each group writes one partial sum.
A second dispatch combines the partials. Compare with an independent sequential sum.

accessibility.text: A two-pass tree reduction with an invented group size of 8, 4 or 2 (not a description of any GPU's execution width). The values are 1, 2, …, n, or 1, −2, 3, … when signs alternate. With the lesson's n = 10 and groups of 8, two groups are needed; the second holds 9 and 10 and six padding slots filled with 0, the identity for addition. Each group adds pairwise in log2(8) = 3 rounds, giving partials 36 and 19, and a second pass adds them to 55, matching the sequential sum. Dropping the incomplete final group instead gives 36: every value is finite and the result is repeatable, yet wrong. Whenever n is a multiple of the group size, both tail rules agree, so boundary tests need sizes that are not multiples. The tree panel shows the last group's slots, with padding slots shaded, and each round's sums.

scenes.title: Bytes, bits and a cycle budget.
scenes.description: Convert a payload in MiB and a link rate in megabits per second into an ideal transfer time, place it in a work cycle with computation and merge, compare a serial schedule with an idealized overlap, and keep retried attempts apart from unique work.

cues.text: A payload in binary mebibytes crosses a link quoted in decimal megabits per second.
Bytes become bits: MiB × 2^20 × 8.
Divide by the link rate in bits per second for the ideal duration. Real overhead only adds to it.
Place compute, transfer and merge in one cycle under the chosen schedule model.
Serial adds all three; ideal overlap takes the longer of compute and transfer, then merge.
Attempts are not unique work. Count logical contributions once.

accessibility.text: A synthetic network and cycle budget. A payload of P MiB is P × 2^20 × 8 bits; over a link of R megabits per second (R × 10^6 bits per second) its ideal duration is P × 2^20 × 8 / (R × 10^6). The lesson's 100 MiB at 200 Mb/s takes 4.194304 seconds, about 4.194, while 100 decimal MB would take 4 seconds. Protocol overhead, congestion and retries can only make it longer. One work cycle has computation, transfer and merge. Serial execution adds them: 8 + 5 + 2 = 15 seconds in the lesson's example. A separately stated model where computation and transfer overlap perfectly and merge cannot overlap gives max(8, 5) + 2 = 10 seconds; that is a model, not evidence that an implementation overlaps. Here the transfer time is computed from the payload and link rate instead of the lesson's round 5 seconds. Sixty logical contributions that each take three attempts show 180 on an attempt counter, yet the unique work is still 60. An upload is not proof of acceptance. All figures are invented for the calculation.

scenes.title: One flat buffer, many readings.
scenes.description: Choose an index (b, t, d) in a (2,3,4) tensor and find its element offset and byte range in the flat row-major buffer. Then decode an offset back into an index, and see the same offset read under a different shape.

cues.text: A (2,3,4) tensor is 24 values in one flat buffer. Predict where index (b, t, d) lives.
Row-major order: the last index moves fastest, so each time step is a run of four features.
Offset = b·12 + t·4 + d, using the strides (12, 4, 1).
Multiply by the element size for the byte range. Offset and allocation size are different quantities.
Reverse it: divide by the strides to decode an offset into (b, t, d).
Read the same offset as shape (2,4,3) and it names a different element. Size checks cannot catch that.

accessibility.text: Tensor indexing with the lesson's shape (2,3,4): two batch entries, three time steps and four features, 24 elements stored in one flat row-major buffer, drawn as two blocks of three rows of four numbered boxes. The element offset of (b, t, d) is b·12 + t·4 + d. The lesson's (1,2,3) has offset 12 + 8 + 3 = 23, the final element, and (0,2,1) has offset 9. With 4-byte FP32 elements the payload is 96 bytes and offset 23 occupies bytes 92 to 95; with a 2-byte format the payload is 48 bytes and the same element occupies bytes 46 and 47. Decoding reverses the arithmetic: offset 17 gives b = 17 div 12 = 1, t = (17 mod 12) div 4 = 1 and d = 17 mod 4 = 1, the lesson's (1,1,1). Read as shape (2,4,3), the same offset names (1,1,2): equal element counts do not make the shapes agree. A scalar of shape () holds one element and a (0,4) tensor holds none.

scenes.title: Average the batch. Watch each example.
scenes.description: Two examples share one weight. Change the weight, the learning rate and the batch reduction, follow the per-example losses and gradients into one update, and compare the batch loss with each example's loss afterwards.

cues.text: Two examples, (x = 1, y = 3) and (x = 2, y = 2), share the weight w. Predict the batch gradient's sign.
Each example has its own residual, half squared loss and gradient r·x.
A mean divides the summed losses and gradients by two; a sum does not. Write the reduction down.
One update: w′ = w − η·(batch gradient).
Recompute each example's loss at w′. The bars compare before (grey) and after.
The batch loss can fall while one example gets worse. Inspect members, not just the average.

accessibility.text: A batch of two examples for prediction = w·x with half squared error: (x = 1, y = 3) and (x = 2, y = 2). Bars show each example's loss before (grey) and after the step. Changing w, η or the reduction updates every value; with η = 0 nothing changes.

scenes.title: Every slot and every use adds.
scenes.description: Run the lesson's tiny reverse-mode engine on u = x·x and z = u + u. Break the multiplication rule, replace += with assignment, or skip the reset and call backward() again, and compare x.grad with the true derivative 4x.

children.text: GRAPH: z = u + u, u = x·x
x·x reads x in two slots
z = u + u uses u twice

cues.text: u = x·x reads x twice; z = u + u uses u twice. Predict dz/dx before running backward.
Forward at x = 2 gives u = 4 and z = 8, saving both multiplication operands.
Backward starts with z.grad = 1. Each use of u adds 1, so u.grad = 2.
Each operand slot of x·x adds the other operand times u.grad: x.grad = 2·x·2 = 4x.
Compare with the true derivative 4x and an independent central difference.
A one-slot rule or = instead of += breaks shared inputs. Skipping the reset makes a repeated call accumulate.

accessibility.text: The lesson's scalar reverse-mode engine on u = x·x and z = u + u. At x = 2 the forward pass gives u = 4 and z = 8. Backward sets z.grad = 1; the addition passes 1 to each of its two operand slots, both of which are u, so with += u.grad = 2. The multiplication passes x·u.grad to each of its two slots, both of which are x, so x.grad = 2·2·2 = 8, matching the derivative 4x and a central difference. A one-slot multiplication rule returns half: the lesson's x·x derivative 2 instead of 4, so x.grad = 4. Replacing += with assignment keeps only the last contribution: u.grad = 1 and x.grad = x = 2. The reference resets every reachable gradient at the start of backward(), so repeated calls give 8 again; without that reset a second call would make u.grad 4 and x.grad 24, and a third 6 and 48. The graph shows each edge's contribution; a faded edge is a slot the broken rule ignores.

scenes.title: A skip path and the right axis.
scenes.description: Stack layers whose branch has slope F′ and compare the derivative through the plain stack with the derivative through residual layers y = x + F(x). Then normalize a token's features alone and inside a batch, per token or over the whole batch.

cues.text: Each layer applies F(x) = F′·x. Predict the derivative through ten layers with F′ = 0.1.
Through the plain stack the local derivatives multiply: F′^L, 0.1^10 = 1e-10.

scenes.title: Look up a row. Add back into it.
scenes.description: Choose the token IDs at three positions, gather their rows from the lesson's four-row embedding table, and add position vectors. Then send gradients back: a row looked up twice must receive both contributions.

cues.text: The table has V = 4 rows of width D = 2: eight parameters however long the batch is.
Each ID selects a row. A repeated ID selects the same row, not a copy.
Gather the rows and add each position's vector, so repeats can differ by position.
Compare positions 0 and 2: same ID, different input once positions are added.
Backward scatters each position's gradient into its row. Repeats must add.
Rows not looked up get no contribution from this lookup. That is not a promise they never change.

scenes.title: A thin update, added beside W.
scenes.description: Build the lesson's rank-one update ΔW = s·B·A, apply it to x through the factors and through the dense matrix, and compare trainable counts by rank. Then start one or both factors at zero and see which factor can receive a gradient.

cues.text: The base W (3×4) stays fixed. LoRA learns B (3×r) and A (r×4); here r = 1.
ΔW = s·B·A is an outer product: every row is a multiple of A.
Apply the factors in order: first A·x, a single number for rank one.
Then Δy = s·B·(A·x), the lesson's [12, −6, 3]. The base output W·x is added separately.
Multiplying by the dense ΔW gives the same vector, at the cost of materializing 12 values.
Each factor's gradient depends on the other. B = 0 with A nonzero: Δy starts at 0 but B learns. Both zero: stuck. s = 0: scaled away.

scenes.title: Same math, different messages.
scenes.description: Split the lesson's matrix product across two workers by output columns or by input features and choose how to combine their partial results. Weight two data replicas by example count. Then follow a two-stage pipeline and choose what stage B sends back.

cues.text: x = [1, 2] times W with rows [1, 3] and [2, 4] is [5, 11]. Two workers share the work.
Split output columns and each worker owns a whole output; split input features and each owns a partial vector.
Column results are concatenated; feature partials must be summed. The operations are not interchangeable.
Data replicas: weight each replica's mean gradient by its example count, (1·2 + 3·6)/4 = 5, not 4.
Pipeline: stage A computes h = w·x and sends it to stage B, which predicts v·h against target 4.
Stage B gets dL/dpred and its own weight gradient.
Stage A needs dL/dh = dL/dpred · v, not B's weight gradient. Check A's resulting dw.

scenes.title: Tile the logits. Keep one denominator.
scenes.description: Size the fp32 logits array and a tile along token rows or vocabulary columns. Then stream the lesson's four logits in two vocabulary tiles with a running maximum and rescaled sum, and compare the cross-entropy with two broken combine rules.

cues.text: A materialized fp32 logits array takes 4·N·V bytes: 32 MiB at N = 1024, V = 8192.
256-row tiles need 8 MiB and stay independent; 256-column tiles need 1 MiB but share one softmax denominator.
Stream the vocabulary: tile 1 has max 1000 and scaled sum 1 + e^−1.
Tile 2 has its own max and scaled sum.
Combine: M = max(m, mt), s = s·e^(m−M) + st·e^(mt−M).
Loss = M + ln s − z_target: 2.440 for the lesson's logits. Skipping the rescale or the other tile changes the objective.
The gradient of the target logit is its globally normalized probability minus one.

scenes.title: Text in, IDs through, text out.
scenes.description: Encode a short text with the lesson's three-symbol vocabulary, read the invented next-token row chosen by the last ID, append greedy choices and decode them. Then swap two tokenizer IDs, or build training targets without the shift, and see which boundary broke.

children.text: THE LAST ID PICKS A ROW

cues.text: The vocabulary is a, b and space (␣) with IDs 0, 1 and 2. Encode the prompt first.
This toy model consults only the last ID: it selects one row of an invented probability table.
Greedy decoding takes the most probable ID in that row.
Decode the chosen ID back to a character and append it. The table itself does not change.
Repeat: each appended token becomes the new last token.
Training pairs shift by one: each input position's target is the following token.

accessibility.text: Tokenization and next-token prediction with the lesson's vocabulary a, b and space (shown as ␣), whose IDs are 0, 1 and 2. The prompt ab␣a encodes to [0, 1, 2, 0]. An invented next-token table, not a trained model, gives one probability row per last ID: after a [0.1, 0.7, 0.2], after b [0.2, 0.2, 0.6], after space [0.8, 0.1, 0.1]. The last ID 0 selects the first row, the greedy choice is ID 1 with probability 0.7, and it decodes to b. Appending b makes ID 1 the last token, so the next greedy choice is a space with probability 0.6, then a. Generation changes the context; it never changes the table. If the tokenizer swaps the IDs of a and b while the table stays the same, the code still runs: a prompt ending in a or b now reads the wrong row, and a prompt ending in a space reads the right row (its ID is unchanged) but decodes the chosen ID 0 as b instead of a. Training pairs come from shifting the sequence: inputs [0, 1, 2] pair with targets [1, 2, 0]. Copying the current token as its own target leaks the answer into the input. IDs are categorical labels, not quantities.

scenes.title: Order the steps. Then judge them.
scenes.description: Run the lesson's one-weight training loop next to a chosen variant: the correct update, a flipped sign, or a gradient buffer that is never cleared. Change the start weight, the learning rate and the number of steps, and see whether the loss alone could tell them apart.

cues.text: Prediction w·x with x = 2 and target 4, half squared error. Predict the first gradient at w = 1.
Step 1: the gradient is −4, so w moves to 1.4 in the reference loop.
Step 2 recomputes the gradient at the new weight (−2.4) and reaches 1.64. A loop that kept the old gradient adds both.
Compare losses: the uncleared buffer reaches 2.04, and its loss is small here.
Judge the transition, not the loss: a wrong update can still lower the loss.

accessibility.text: A one-weight training loop with the lesson's numbers: prediction w·x with input 2, target 4, half squared error and learning rate 0.1, starting at w = 1. The reference loop subtracts the learning rate times the fresh gradient: the first gradient is −4, so w becomes 1.4; at that weight the gradient is −2.4, so w becomes 1.64, and the loss falls from 2 to 0.72 and then 0.2592. Adding instead of subtracting sends w to 0.6 after one step, where the loss is 3.92. Keeping the first gradient in an uncleared buffer adds it to the second: the second step uses −6.4 and sends w from 1.4 to 2.04. Its loss, 0.0032, is lower than the reference's, yet the state transition is wrong: loss improvement does not validate the algorithm. The verdict names the cause. With w0 = 2 every gradient is zero, so all three loops agree and the bug is hidden by the zero gradient; with one step the uncleared buffer has nothing stale in it yet, so it agrees with the reference for that reason. The number line shows each loop's weights from −2 to 4 (values beyond are pinned to the ends), with the target weight 2 marked.

scenes.description: Project the lesson's two-token X into queries, keys and values with three learned matrices, then read the score grid row by row. Swap the order of Q and K, try a symmetric fixture, and drop one route from the input gradient.

cues.text: X has one row per token. Wq, Wk and Wv are learned 2×2 matrices: twelve weights.
Q = X·Wq, K = X·Wk and V = X·Wv: the same rows, three different projections.
Score S[i, j] compares query i with key j: S = Q·Kᵀ.
Row i is what query i sees across the candidate source positions.
Swapping Q and K gives the transpose. A symmetric fixture hides that mistake.
Backward: X receives a contribution through Q, K and V. Dropping one route corrupts ∂X.

scenes.title: Returning is not finishing.
scenes.description: On an invented timeline the host submits work and returns while the device is still running. Move the timer's start and stop boundaries, add earlier queued work, and compare what the timer reads with the completion latency. Then permute one output row and see why that is not rounding.

cues.text: A Python call can enqueue device work and return before that work finishes.
The host spends s milliseconds submitting: 0.2 ms in the lesson's invented timeline.
The device runs the work afterwards, behind anything queued earlier; the result is ready at 5.2 ms.
The timer reads the gap between its start and stop boundaries.
Completion latency needs a sync before starting and a sync before stopping: s + d.
Name the boundary that made a reading wrong. A permuted output row is a semantic bug, not rounding.

Waiting for earlier work before starting and syncing on the device before stopping reads 5.2 ms, the completion latency s + d. If earlier work is still queued and the timer starts immediately, a synced stop also counts that earlier work: with 3 ms queued it reads 8 ms. Starting immediately happens to read the right value when nothing is queued, or when the earlier work drains before submission ends; the verdict says so. Separately, the lesson's product of A = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] and B = [[2, 0], [1, 2]] is [[4, 4], [10, 8]]. A kernel that writes the second row as [8, 10] has maximum error 2: that is a permutation of indices, not floating-point rounding, and no tolerance should accept it. scenes.title: Count every state. Find the floor.
scenes.description: Stack the lesson's fictional training state against an 18 GiB working budget: parameters, gradients, optimizer buffers and live activations. Shrink activations or store weights at half size, count only parameters by mistake, then speed up the GPU part of a step and see where Amdahl's law stops you.

cues.text: A fictional machine has 24 GiB. Predict whether training state of 5 + 5 + 10 + 3 GiB fits.
Reserve 6 GiB for the system and other work: the budget is 18 GiB.
Training needs parameters, gradients, optimizer buffers and live activations: 23 GiB.
Counting only the parameters would report 5 GiB and plenty of headroom.

scenes.title: Hold the input until its backward.
scenes.description: Schedule three activations through a ready queue with a limited activation cache, an invented return delay for each, and an accumulation threshold for the local optimizer. scenes.description: Split a fictional transformer into head, body and tail by two boundaries and read how many blocks each role constructs. Size the head's activation payload for two widths, then normalize the tail's loss by positions or, mistakenly, by every logit.

An archived head record reports output shape [4, 800, 32]: 102,400 values.

scenes.description: Compare candidate outputs with the lesson's reference [1, 2, 3, 4]: a permutation, a single spike, a constant bias, an empty result and an exact copy. Sum and norm are identical; so are finiteness, repeatability and the hash of the wrong vector.
